headline: The market is now punishing AI spenders that burn cash: Amazon and Intel sank after hours and Nasdaq 100 futures are down 2% to 2.5%, while Exxon and Chevron beat on refining and Brent rose to about $117.6 after a Hormuz tanker attack.
summary: The dashboard is still on Oct 28 closes (prices_as_of 2026-10-28, refresh running), so every close below is the Oct 29 close from Massive, the price source of record. On Oct 29 Alphabet fell 12.64%, its worst day on record, the S&P 500 slipped 0.3% to 7,720.39 and the 10 year eased to 4.937% (Massive, AP via Barchart, TheStreet). After the close Amazon missed and showed negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion over 12 months, Intel guided low, and before the open Nasdaq 100 futures were down 2% to 2.5%, with Asian markets down 2% to 3.5% (CNBC, Focus Taiwan). Exxon and Chevron beat on record refining and were up 1% to 2% premarket, while Brent rose 2.4% to $117.62 after a tanker was hit in the Strait of Hormuz (CNBC, Reuters). WST confirmed its swing breakout on 3.35 times normal volume, but MSFT did not: it traded above 533.42 and closed at 530.14. The ECB and the Bank of Japan both held; the US midterms are Tuesday and Brazil's rate decision is Nov 3 to 4.

regime.why: Money is rotating, not leaving: the S&P 500 fell only 0.3% on Oct 29 and Dow futures are slightly higher, while AI spenders and chip stocks take the hit. The AI buildout is still growing (Amazon will spend more in 2027), but buyers now demand cash returns, and the 10 year near 4.9% keeps that bar high. Oil is the other risk: Brent is up about 14% in October with the midterms four days away.

signals.title: Amazon and Intel join Alphabet: the market sells AI spenders that burn cash, and Microsoft's swing trigger failed
signals.since_yesterday: Amazon missed and posted negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion over 12 months; Intel guided low; Alphabet closed down 12.64%. Correction: Microsoft cut its capex forecast to $170 billion from $175 billion; it was not a 2027 increase.
signals.what_happened: Amazon's Q3 EPS was $1.89 against $1.96 expected and revenue $201.94 billion against $202.31 billion; AWS grew 39% to $45.98 billion, but ad revenue of $19.64 billion missed. Q3 capex was $77.3 billion against $58.7 billion expected, it kept its $220 billion 2026 plan, said it will spend 'meaningfully more in 2027', and trailing free cash flow was negative $42.4 billion (CNBC). Intel guided Q4 revenue to $15 billion to $16 billion and EPS of 25 cents, against $17.1 billion and 43 cents expected, citing weak PCs (CNBC). Before the open Amazon was down 6% to 7% and Intel about 24% (CNBC). On Oct 29 Alphabet closed at 283.82, down 12.64% on 139.7 million shares, and Amazon had already fallen 4.25% to 243.79 before its report (Massive). Microsoft opened at 540.22, traded as high as 541.29, then closed at 530.14 on 39.3 million shares, 1.86 times its 50 day average (Massive). Correction to yesterday: CNBC reports Microsoft cut its capex forecast for the year to $170 billion from $175 billion, and both Microsoft and Alphabet capex came in under estimates.
signals.so_what: The spending is not stopping: Amazon will spend more in 2027 and its chip unit grows triple digits, which keeps money flowing to chips, memory, power and builders. What changed is the price of that spending. Three of the four biggest spenders now show shrinking or negative free cash flow, and the ECB's Lagarde said their bond issuance is helping push long term rates up worldwide (CNBC). Second order: suppliers sold off with the spenders (Micron -4.98%, Arm and Nvidia lower premarket) even though their orders are intact; that is a sentiment hit, not a demand hit, until a spender cuts. Third order: if rates stay high and stock buyers keep punishing cash burn, 2028 budgets get trimmed, and that would hit suppliers last. What would make this wrong: Apple and Nvidia showing strong demand in the next two weeks.
signals.for_you: Swing: MSFT failed. It closed at 530.14, under the 533.42 entry, even on 1.86 times volume; the dashboard's newer setup (entry 552.26, stop 530.96 on Oct 28 data) is also broken by that close. No MSFT swing. Long term: MSFT is 'Buy zone now' and closed 0.7% above its 423.12 to 526.49 zone; a weak open could put it inside. If you add, a small first tranche after the open settles, not at the bell. AMZN is Wait with its zone (261.15 to 262.77) above the price. INTC is 'Accumulate on pullback', but a 24% gap is a falling knife; no buy or put until it stops falling.

signals.title: Exxon and Chevron beat on record refining; both swings are at their 2R targets
signals.since_yesterday: They reported: adjusted EPS of $4.23 for Exxon and $5.28 for Chevron both beat, and both were up premarket.
signals.what_happened: Exxon earned $15.4 billion, or $3.72 a share; adjusted EPS was $4.23 against $4.08 expected, on revenue of $113.2 billion against $103.1 billion (LSEG via CNBC). For the first time in at least six years Exxon earned more from refining than from oil and gas production, its Gulf Coast refineries ran at 100%, it cut debt by $8 billion in the quarter and set a $20 billion buyback for 2027, the same as the last two years (Reuters). Chevron earned $9.9 billion; adjusted EPS was $5.28 against $4.89 expected on $67.8 billion of revenue; refining profit rose more than 300% to $4.9 billion and US refineries ran at 98% (CNBC). Both are using the windfall to pay down debt rather than raise payouts (Reuters). Premarket: Exxon up about 1.5% to 2%, Chevron about 1% to 2% (CNBC, Reuters). Oct 29 closes: XOM 183.29 on 0.84 times its 50 day volume, CVX 231.46 on 0.67 times (Massive).
signals.so_what: The war is paying the refiners more than the drillers: Russian and Saudi refinery attacks took fuel capacity offline, and US plants are the backstop. That windfall depends on diesel staying scarce, which makes it more fragile than it looks: a peace deal or a Russian refinery recovery would shrink margins fast. Paying down debt instead of raising buybacks says management does not trust these prices to last. Who pays: truckers, airlines and farmers through diesel. What would make this wrong: a quick reopening of Saudi and Russian refineries.
signals.for_you: Swing, by the numbers on Oct 29 closes: XOM is 1.90R above its 169.99 entry (risk 7.00 a share) and CVX is 1.70R above 218.23 (risk 7.78), both on light volume (my calculation, Massive). The 2R targets are XOM 183.99 and CVX 233.79; premarket prices sit at or above them. The plan says take the target: sell at or near 2R at the open, or sell at least half and move the stop on the rest to the entry (169.99, 218.23). Do not hold full size into the Nov 3 vote. COP (150.03, about 1.32R) and EOG (162.22, about 1.19R) stay open with stops 135.75 and 147.98; volume was light at 0.79 and 0.84 times. Check their report dates before holding into next week.

signals.title: A tanker was hit in Hormuz and Houthis claim strikes on Saudi refineries: Brent near $117.6 before the midterms
signals.since_yesterday: Yesterday's dip on peace feelers reversed: a tanker was hit by explosive devices Friday and Brent is up 2.4%.
signals.what_happened: A tanker in the Strait of Hormuz was hit by explosive devices attached by a small boat on Oct 30 (UKMTO via Reuters). On Oct 29 Houthi rebels said they struck Saudi Aramco's Ras Tanura and Rabigh refineries and a site at Abqaiq (Reuters). Brent for December rose $2.74 to $117.62 at 10:45 GMT and WTI $2.18 to $104.18; Brent is up nearly 14% in October (Reuters). Qatari mediators returned to Tehran, and Iran has not answered a letter from Vice President Vance (Reuters). Gulf crude exports averaged 24.6 million barrels a day in the week to Oct 18, above the pre war level (Kpler via Al Jazeera). Exxon and Chevron cancelled executive trips to next week's ADIPEC show in Abu Dhabi (Reuters). Goldman sees $120 if ship attacks escalate and about $80 if exports normalize (Economic Times).
signals.so_what: Crude is flowing again, yet prices rise, because the scarce thing is now refined fuel and safe passage, not crude barrels. That is why refiners, not drillers, are winning. Traders are long into Nov 3 (Kpler via Reuters), so the risk runs both ways: a strike after the vote lifts oil, a deal or a quiet week could drop it fast as those longs sell. OPEC+ meets this weekend (Kpler via Reuters).
signals.for_you: Swing: take the plan on XOM and CVX; do not add oil names into Tuesday. Airlines DAL and UAL pay for jet fuel; DAL is on the Buy zone list at 81.64 (inside 74.44 to 82.75), but an oil spike next week is a real risk to it; wait. Puts: none on energy.

signals.title: Central banks lean hawkish: the ECB debated a hike and Lagarde will leave; the BOJ says inflation is at target
signals.what_happened: The ECB held its deposit rate at 2.5% on Oct 29; Lagarde said a hike was debated, and markets price about a 67% chance of a December hike. Euro area inflation is 3.8%, the highest since September 2023 (CNBC). Lagarde announced she will step down on Feb 7, 2027 (CNBC). On Oct 30 the Bank of Japan held at 1.25% in an 8 to 1 vote, with one member wanting 1.5%, and said for the first time since 2013 that inflation is 'generally consistent' with its 2% target (CNBC). Dutch December gas jumped to 101.63 euros, the highest since late 2022, and France's economy shrank 0.1% in Q3 (CNBC).
signals.so_what: The Fed, the ECB and the BOJ all held this week, but all three lean toward hiking, and none is cutting. Rising rates in Japan matter most for US stocks: a stronger yen can force investors who borrowed cheap yen to sell US assets. Europe faces a winter energy squeeze with gas storage near 75%. What would make this wrong: a sharp drop in oil after the midterms.
signals.for_you: Puts: the 10 year at 4.937% is the bar a put premium must beat on an annual basis. No direct trade. Watch the yen; a quick rise has hit US tech for a day or two before.

signals.title: Asian chip markets fell 2% to 3.5%; memory is down 14% in October
signals.since_yesterday: The Samsung story turned into a sector selloff: the KOSPI fell 3.48% and the Taiex 2.49% after Amazon and Intel.
signals.what_happened: On Oct 30 the KOSPI fell 3.48% to 5,730.74, with SK hynix down about 6.4% and Samsung about 3.5% during the session; the Nikkei fell 2.12% (CNBC). The Taiex fell 2.49% to 45,211.83 with a net NT$112.47 billion of foreign selling, and TSMC fell 1.86% (Focus Taiwan). The Roundhill Memory ETF is down 14% in October (CNBC). In New York on Oct 29 MU fell 4.98% to 934.27 and the SK hynix ADR (SKHY) 1.58% to 162.09 (Massive).
signals.so_what: Memory makers said this week that supply stays tight into 2028, so this is a price reset on fear about the spenders, not a demand break. Foreign money leaving Taiwan and Korea at this pace usually takes more than a day to finish. The second order risk: if memory prices keep rising while spenders slow, the spenders' margins get squeezed from both sides.
signals.for_you: No chase and no puts in memory or Asian chip names this week. MU has no confirmed setup.

signals.title: Brazil fell a fourth day and the real weakened; correction on what the rate market expects
signals.since_yesterday: The Ibovespa lost 1.06% to 169,186 and the real fell 0.76% to R$5.39. Earlier briefs said markets price a Selic hike; sources disagree.
signals.what_happened: The Ibovespa fell 1.06% to 169,186 on Oct 29, a fourth straight loss, and the dollar rose 0.76% to R$5.39 on worries about Lula's spending (Agencia Brasil). In New York EWZ fell 1.43% to 33.14, BBD 3.66% to 2.63 and ITUB 0.41% to 7.37, while NU rose 0.67% to 12.05 (Massive). Correction: before the vote, economists expected a 0.25 point cut on Nov 4 (Focus survey closed Oct 23); after Lula won, rate futures jumped and analysts now debate a pause at 13.75% (Estadao). An earlier InfoMoney report said a hike is priced. The weight of sources points to a pause, not a hike.
signals.so_what: Either a pause or a hike is worse than the cut the market expected a week ago, so banks and lenders lose either way. The real weakening again matters more than the stock drop: it shows foreign money still leaving.
signals.for_you: No Brazil buys, swings or new puts before Nov 4. NU is Wait at 12.05, 8.0% under its 13.10 line (my calculation). If you sold the EWZ Nov 20 $37 put from an earlier brief, it is 10.4% in the money at 33.14; with no verdict, the rule is no roll.

signals.title: The biggest crypto hack yet: Binance says $6.3 billion was hit
signals.what_happened: Binance said a breach had an estimated $6.3 billion impact, with about $3 billion frozen so far, and pledged to cover all losses; it suspended deposits and withdrawals (CNBC). Circle and Tether froze a combined $2.54 billion linked to the incident, and bitcoin fell below $78,000 (CNBC). On Oct 29 Mastercard rose 4.16% to 635.70 and Visa 2.48% to 410.54 after Mastercard beat estimates (briefs.co), while COIN fell 1.07% (Massive).
signals.so_what: A hack this size invites regulation and pulls trading volume from exchanges for a while, which hurts COIN and HOOD's crypto revenue. Stablecoin issuers freezing funds shows the control that regulators wanted, which helps the case for regulated rails. Card networks keep winning on consumer spending.
signals.for_you: No crypto trades this week. MA is 'Buy zone now' on Oct 28 data but closed 5.8% above its 517.30 to 601.09 zone: no buy at this price. HOOD stays Wait.

cycle.quadrant_why: Q3 GDP grew at a 3.4% pace and September core PCE was 3.1% (AP, FXStreet, Oct 29). Euro area inflation is 3.8% and the Bank of Japan now says inflation is at its 2% target (CNBC). Brent is near $117.6 (Reuters).
cycle.short_term_debt_cycle: Tightening, late. The Fed, the ECB and the BOJ all held this week, and each had members pushing for a hike; markets price about a 67% chance of an ECB hike in December (CNBC). The US 10 year eased to 4.937% (TheStreet).
cycle.long_term_debt_cycle: Late. The AI build is now partly debt funded: Amazon's trailing free cash flow is negative $42.4 billion and Alphabet's quarter was negative $9.07 billion (CNBC), and Lagarde says hyperscaler bonds are pushing up long term rates worldwide (CNBC). France is fighting deficits and unrest.
cycle.big_cycle: External order: the Iran war, a Hormuz tanker attack and Houthi strikes on Saudi refineries. Internal order: US midterms on Nov 3, unrest in France, and the ECB president leaving in February. Technology: the AI spending race now tests whether the spenders can fund it.
tailwinds: Amazon will spend more in 2027, so orders for chips, memory, power and builders keep growing.
Refining and card network profits are strong (Exxon, Chevron, Mastercard).
headwinds: Investors punish AI spenders that burn cash (Alphabet -12.64%, Amazon and Intel down premarket).
Oil near $117 and three central banks leaning toward hikes.

history.when: July to December 2008, the oil spike and crash
history.what: Brent spot peaked near $144 a barrel in early July 2008 and fell to about $34 by late December (EIA daily Brent spot).
history.lesson: Prices driven by fear of scarcity can reverse faster than anyone expects once the fear or the demand fades. Refining windfalls are even more fragile than crude prices. Take the 2R on oil swings.

history.when: June 1999 to May 2000, Fed hikes into the tech capex boom
history.what: The Fed raised its target from 4.75% to 6.50% while companies spent heavily on internet and telecom gear (Federal Reserve rate history).
history.lesson: Rising rates first punish the spenders with weak cash flow, and later their suppliers. This week three of the four biggest AI spenders were sold for cash burn; the suppliers are next only if orders get cut.

source.title: Federal Reserve open market operations: historical target rate changes (Federal Reserve)

cycle.differences: In 2008 demand collapsed with the financial crisis; today demand is steady and the shortage is in refining and safe shipping. In 1999 the spenders were young and unprofitable; today they are the richest firms in the world, but they are now borrowing to keep pace.
cycle.for_you: Swing: take 2R on XOM and CVX; WST is the one confirmed new trigger; no MSFT. Puts: none pass the rules today; the bar is 4.937%. Long term: do not buy into a 2% Nasdaq gap; let the open settle and favor calm names inside their zones (JPM, PYPL).

principle.text: Weigh the second and third order consequences of your decisions, not just the first (Principles).
principle.applied: First order, Amazon spending more is good for chip suppliers. Second order, the cash burn pushes up borrowing costs and lowers what buyers pay for the spenders. Third order, if that lasts, 2028 budgets shrink and the suppliers feel it last. That is why the supplier selloff is a watch, not a buy, today.
